summary: Defines a DHCPv6 mechanism for assigning link-layer (MAC) addresses. It is aimed at settings such as large virtualization deployments, where many devices are created automatically and random assignment could cause address collisions. A server hands out addresses so duplicates are avoided.

eli5.summary: When a huge number of virtual computers are created, each needs a unique hardware name. This lets a central helper hand out names so no two collide.

questions: how to assign mac addresses with dhcpv6
how does dhcpv6 hand out mac address blocks
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 server can hand out blocks of MAC addresses to hypervisors and devices, so large fleets avoid address collisions.

tldr.problem: When new devices or virtual machines are created automatically at large scale, giving each a random link-layer address risks collisions, and manufacturer-assigned addresses are not always possible or needed.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DHCPv6 options, IA_LL and LLADDR, let a client ask a server for a block of link-layer addresses and then renew or release it using the normal DHCPv6 message exchanges.
tldr.outcome: A server can allocate locally unique MAC addresses inside an administrative domain. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Recommended T1 / T2
facts.value: 0.5 and 0.8 of the shortest valid lifetime

today: RFC 8947 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2020, and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. A companion option for choosing the address quadrant is defined in RFC 8948.

sections.title: Why Assign MAC Addresses with DHCPv6
sections.content:
Some deployments create devices in huge numbers: virtual machines (VMs) spun up on a massive scale, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Picking a link-layer address at random does not scale well because of the risk of a collision. The IoT case also has a second worry: the huge number of devices could strain the IEEE's available global OUI address space.

These devices usually do not need a globally unique address. A mechanism that avoids conflicts inside one administrative domain is enough. RFC 8947 therefore extends DHCPv6 (RFC 8415) so that it can allocate locally unique MAC addresses, reusing DHCPv6's existing servers, clients, relays, leasequery and failover.

The design is meant to work for any link-layer address type, but some details are specific to IEEE 802 48-bit MAC addresses. IEEE has also been developing its own protocols for assigning local addresses (IEEE 802.1CQ), which the RFC notes may serve as an alternative.
sections.eli5: If everyone in a huge school picked a nickname at random, two kids might pick the same one. It is safer to have the office hand out nicknames from a list.

sections.title: Proxy Client and Direct Client Modes
sections.content:
The RFC targets two scenarios, and the protocol works the same way in both.

In proxy client mode, an entity such as a hypervisor acts as the DHCP client and asks the servers for an address block. It does not use those addresses itself. It hands them to the VMs it creates. Over time its address use tends to grow, although addresses of deleted VMs may be reused.

In direct client mode, the device asks for an address for its own use, which is the IoT case. On first boot, for each interface, it uses a temporary address to send its first DHCP packets and asks for a single address. Once the server assigns one, the device abandons the temporary address and uses the leased one.

A direct-mode client that has no globally unique link-layer address on any interface MUST NOT use a link-layer-based DUID. Also, a switch that restricts link-layer address changes may block this use unless the administrator adjusts its configuration.
sections.eli5: A school bus driver might collect a stack of name tags for all the kids on the bus (proxy). A single new kid might just ask for one name tag for themselves (direct).

sections.title: Design Assumptions and Mechanism Overview
sections.content:
A hypervisor may use thousands of addresses over time. Listing one option per address, as DHCPv6 does for IPv6 addresses or prefixes, would not work well. So the mechanism works on address blocks: a first address plus a count of extra addresses. A single address is a block with zero extra addresses. A device that only wants link-layer addresses does not need to support full DHCP, and need not handle IPv6 addresses or prefixes.

The client sends a Solicit with an IA_LL option. Servers answer with an Advertise (or a Reply if Rapid Commit is requested and honored). The client picks one, sends a Request if needed, and the chosen server assigns the addresses in a Reply. Clients SHOULD use Rapid Commit to get addresses in a two-message exchange when possible.

Renewal follows the T1 and T2 timers, and the client stops using an address when its valid lifetime expires. A server can disable renewals by sending infinity as T1 and T2, and can make an assignment permanent with an infinite valid lifetime. Confirm and Information-request are not used. Decline should in principle never be needed, except in one case described below.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing every name on its own slip, the office hands over a numbered range, like "names 10 through 20". The kid asks, the office answers, and the kid checks in again later to keep them.

sections.title: Requesting, Renewing and Releasing
sections.content:
Requesting. The client puts an LLADDR option, which names the link-layer type and length, inside an IA_LL option in a Solicit. For Ethernet (type 1) and IEEE 802 networks (type 6) it sets the address field to all zeroes if it has no hint, or to a specific starting address. The extra-addresses field is 0 for one address, or the block size minus 1. The server may offer a different start or a smaller block than requested, and the client MUST use what the Reply returns. Addresses in an Advertise must not be used until they come back in a Reply. If the server has nothing to give it returns the status NoAddrsAvail. A server that does not understand IA_LL ignores it, and the client treats that as NoAddrsAvail.

Renewing. After T1 the client sends Renew with the block; after T2 it falls back to Rebind. The server MUST NOT shrink or expand a block, and once a block has a non-zero valid lifetime its size, start and end MUST NOT change. To get more addresses, the client MUST use a different IAID, creating another container.

Releasing. A client MUST release a block in its entirety with a Release. If it is releasing the address it is itself using, it MUST stop using it first and send the message from another address, such as the one it used to start DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: You ask for a batch of names and take whatever the office gives you. If you want more later, you open a second request. When you are done you give back the whole batch at once.

sections.title: The IA_LL and LLADDR Options
sections.content:
There is one container option and one option per address block.

The IA_LL option (option code 138) carries an IAID, T1, T2 and a list of encapsulated options. Its option-len is 12 plus the length of the options field. The IAID number space is separate from IA_NA, IA_TA and IA_PD. A message may hold several IA_LL options, each with a unique IAID. Clients MUST set T1 and T2 to 0 and servers ignore them. From a server, recommended values are 0.5 and 0.8 of the shortest valid lifetime in the IA. If T1 is greater than T2 and both are non-zero, the client discards the IA_LL option.

The LLADDR option (option code 139) carries a 2-octet link-layer-type (a valid IANA hardware type), a 2-octet link-layer-len, the first address, a 4-octet extra-addresses count and a 4-octet valid-lifetime, followed by optional sub-options (none are defined). With a 6-octet address and no extra options the option-len is 18. As an example, the first address 02:04:06:08:0a with extra-addresses 3 designates four addresses ending in 02:04:06:08:0d. Clients set valid-lifetime to 0 and servers ignore it. The value 0xffffffff means infinity. If a client omits LLADDR in a Solicit or Request, the server treats it as a request for a single address with no hint.
sections.eli5: The IA_LL is the folder and each LLADDR is a sheet inside it saying "start here, and give me this many names".

sections.title: How a Server Picks Addresses
sections.content:
A server picks addresses by the policy its administrator sets and the rules of the address space. It SHOULD work out the client's link as in Section 13.1 of RFC 8415.

For IEEE 802 MAC addresses:

  • Administrators SHOULD follow the IEEE 802 rules for the unicast address pools: only space reserved for local use, or authorized by its assignee, may be used.
  • Servers MUST NOT allow a pool that crosses the boundary of 2^(42) bits for 48-bit addresses. This avoids problems with changes in the first octet and its special bits. Clients MUST reject such a block by declining it, which is the one case where Decline is needed.
  • A server MAY use options from a relay or client to choose the quadrant of the local address space, for example those in RFC 8948.
sections.eli5: The office has rules about which name lists are allowed, and it never gives out a batch that straddles the line between two lists.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security of this mechanism rests on DHCPv6 itself. RFC 8415 notes that DHCP lacks end-to-end encryption between clients and servers, so hijacking, tampering and eavesdropping are possible. If not every party on a link obtains addresses from the server's space, two devices could end up with the same address, though that risk exists even without DHCP.

Servers SHOULD consider options to limit the number of addresses given to a client, in one request and in total. The RFC admits this does not stop a bad actor pretending to be many clients and consuming all addresses.

On privacy, the assigned address is exposed to anyone who can listen on the link, and those who can see the DHCP exchange can link the client's identity (its DUID) to the address. The RFC points to RFC 7844 for anonymity profiles, and says servers and hypervisors should consider the implications of assigning addresses sequentially, which is generally only a link-local concern.
sections.eli5: Anyone listening in on the hallway can hear which name went to which kid, and a trickster could pretend to be many kids to grab all the names.

sections.title: Background: IEEE 802c Local Address Quadrants
sections.content:
The original IEEE 802 specifications set aside half of the 48-bit MAC address space for local use, with the U/L bit set to 1 and no imposed structure. In 2017 IEEE Std 802c defined an optional Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) that splits that space into four quadrants.

  • 01, Extended Local (ELI): based on a 24-bit Company ID assigned by the IEEE Registration Authority.
  • 11, Standard Assigned (SAI): assigned by a protocol specified in an IEEE 802 standard; 44 bits are available.
  • 00, Administratively Assigned (AAI): assigned locally; 44 bits are available. Addresses starting 33-33 should not be assigned, since IPv6 multicast uses them.
  • 10, Reserved: for future use; it may be used like AAI but future specifications could define incompatible uses.
sections.eli5: The locally made names are split into four zones, each with its own rules for who gets to hand out names there.

messages.label: Advertise
messages.note: Offers addresses. A Reply is sent instead if Rapid Commit is honored.

messages.label: Request
messages.note: Copies the LLADDR from the chosen Advertise.

messages.label: Reply
messages.note: Assigns the block; the client may now use it.

fields.name: link-layer-type
fields.desc: A valid IANA hardware type, such as 1 for Ethernet.

fields.name: link-layer-len
fields.desc: Length in octets of the address field; typically 6.

fields.name: extra-addresses
fields.desc: Number of additional addresses after the first; 0 for a single address.

fields.name: valid-lifetime
fields.desc: Valid lifetime in seconds; clients send 0.

items.label: ELI
items.desc: Extended Local Identifier, based on an assigned Company ID.

items.label: SAI
items.desc: Standard Assigned Identifier, assigned by an IEEE 802 protocol.
